title: Human Factors
summary: Recognize how physiology, workload, and judgment can undermine an otherwise legal flight.
objectives: Distinguish medical eligibility from fitness for today’s flight.
Connect symptoms to oxygen, pressure, sensory, and workload mechanisms.
Use decisions and cockpit practices that interrupt an unsafe chain.

sections.title: Medical eligibility and fitness today
sections.body:
A medical certificate documents an eligibility determination. It does not guarantee that you are fit for every flight during its validity. Illness, medication, poor sleep, stress, alcohol, and dehydration can change performance between examinations. Use IMSAFE to discuss those personal factors, then use PAVE to consider the pilot, aircraft, environment, and external pressures together.

An Aviation Medical Examiner handles medical examinations through the FAA process. A special issuance may permit certification with a condition requiring additional evaluation or monitoring. A Statement of Demonstrated Ability addresses certain stable conditions through demonstrated capability. Neither is permission to ignore new symptoms. The applicable medical or alternative qualification depends on the operation and the pilot’s eligibility.
sections.deep:
Why it matters: medical qualification and self-assessment solve different problems. The examination is periodic; operational risk changes continuously. A pilot may meet a minimum legal requirement while lacking adequate alertness for turbulence, unfamiliar airspace, or a demanding approach. When a condition or medication creates uncertainty, obtain aviation-medical advice before flying. A passenger’s schedule does not restore physiological reserve.

Apply it: change the departure, use another pilot, simplify the flight, or cancel before fatigue becomes an airborne problem.

sections.title: Hypoxia, breathing, and carbon monoxide
sections.body:
Hypoxia means inadequate oxygen at the tissues. Hypoxic hypoxia begins with insufficient oxygen pressure available to the lungs. Hypemic hypoxia limits blood carriage, as with carbon monoxide exposure. Stagnant hypoxia limits circulation. Histotoxic hypoxia prevents cells from using available oxygen effectively. The oxygen percentage in ordinary air remains roughly constant with altitude, while its partial pressure falls.

Headache, impaired judgment, unusual confidence, slowed responses, or visual deterioration deserve action; a person may feel well while performing poorly. Hyperventilation has a different mechanism: breathing removes carbon dioxide faster than the body produces it. Tingling and lightheadedness can resemble hypoxia.
sections.deep:
Do not diagnose uncertain symptoms by removing oxygen. At altitude, use the appropriate oxygen equipment, verify delivery, control breathing, and arrange a safe descent according to the aircraft procedures and situation. Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless; cabin heat may introduce exhaust contamination after a system failure. Follow the aircraft emergency procedure, obtain fresh air, use oxygen if available, land promptly, and obtain medical evaluation. A routine pulse oximeter can be misleading during carbon monoxide exposure.

The useful distinction is where oxygen delivery fails, because simply increasing cabin airflow does not correct every cause.

sections.title: Pressure changes, sickness, and physical reserve
sections.body:
As outside pressure falls in a climb, trapped gas expands. During descent, increasing pressure requires the middle ear and sinuses to equalize. A cold or nasal inflammation may obstruct that process. Pain is a warning, and forcing the issue through a rapid descent can worsen injury. Prevention and sound medical advice are more dependable than trying an unfamiliar decongestant before departure.

Motion sickness arises from conflicting sensory information. A student may first become quiet, pale, or inattentive. Reduce workload, provide ventilation, shorten the lesson, and land when appropriate. Fatigue, heat, dehydration, and sustained stress further reduce the attention available for flying.
sections.deep:
After scuba diving: dissolved nitrogen can form bubbles when pressure decreases. FAA guidance recommends at least 12 hours before flight to actual altitudes up to 8,000 feet after a dive not requiring decompression stops, and at least 24 hours after a dive requiring them. Before flight above 8,000 feet, allow at least 24 hours after any scuba dive. These are actual flight altitudes, not cabin altitudes. Diving-specific or medical advice may be more restrictive.

A conservative waiting plan belongs before the trip; symptoms during a flight are an emergency, not an invitation to finish the itinerary.

sections.title: Why your senses can disagree
sections.body:
The inner ear detects accelerations well but is a poor long-term attitude reference without reliable visual cues. A slow bank can go unnoticed; rolling level may then feel like a bank the other way. Moving the head during a sustained turn can create a powerful false tumbling sensation. Acceleration may feel like pitching up, tempting an unsafe nose-down input.

The eyes also need interpretation. Sloping clouds can become a false horizon. A narrow runway or an upsloping runway can make the aircraft seem higher than it is. Featureless dark terrain removes familiar approach-height cues. An isolated light may seem to wander when stared at for a long time.
sections.deep:
Why: the brain combines several imperfect signals rather than measuring attitude directly. When a familiar cue disappears, confidence in the remaining sensation may increase even while accuracy decreases. Use a disciplined instrument cross-check when external references are unreliable. An instrument-qualified pilot must still remain proficient; instruments cannot help if they are ignored or misread.

Teach it: ask the student to describe the instrument indications that would distinguish an actual climb from a false pitch-up sensation. Conduct demonstrations only within a planned, safe training environment and the instructor’s control.

sections.title: Attention, bias, and practical decisions
sections.body:
Attention is limited. A minor radio problem can absorb enough of it to cause a major flight-path error. First keep the airplane controlled, then establish a safe navigation plan, and communicate as workload permits. Use available resources: ATC, another qualified pilot, an autopilot used correctly, a diversion airport, or simply more time.

Expectation bias means perceiving what you expected. Confirmation bias means favoring information that supports an existing belief. Hearing one traffic call and seeing one airplane does not prove they refer to the same aircraft. Deliberately seek a second check: position, altitude, direction, distance, or a repeated instruction.
sections.deep:
A usable decision cycle is to detect the change, assess its significance, choose an outcome, act, and reassess. PAVE helps identify risks; it does not produce a numerical permission slip. Hazardous attitudes also need an actionable correction: slow down impulsive decisions, reject the idea that experience prevents accidents, accept useful rules, and remember that changing a plan is an available action.

Scenario: deteriorating visibility plus fuel uncertainty and a waiting passenger is a combined problem. A timely diversion can remove several pressures at once. Waiting for each individual risk to reach a legal limit can eliminate the remaining options.

sections.title: Instructor habits, alcohol, and medication
sections.body:
Make control ownership explicit with a positive exchange and visual confirmation. During taxi, runway operations, and other high-workload phases, keep conversation relevant to the task. The instructor must protect the flight while teaching; two people looking down at the same display do not provide two independent safety checks.

Under 14 CFR 91.17, a crewmember may not act or attempt to act within eight hours after drinking, while under the influence, while using an impairing drug, or with an alcohol concentration 0.04 or greater. Passing eight hours or having a lower concentration does not override impairment. Prescription status does not make a medication compatible with flying.
sections.deep:
Training application: introduce distractions progressively and deliberately, with a clear safety margin. Evaluate whether the learner recognizes the distraction and postpones a lower-priority task. Avoid demonstrations that create a real loss of control or runway hazard merely to prove a point.

The passenger provision in 91.17 has an emergency exception and distinguishes a medical patient under proper care. Teach the actual rule rather than an absolute prohibition stripped of its exceptions. For medication, consider the underlying condition, side effects, interactions, and FAA medical guidance together; do not suggest stopping prescribed treatment without the treating clinician.

teachBack: Explain how a valid medical certificate and a safe go/no-go decision answer different questions.
A passenger becomes confused at altitude. Explain why slowing breathing and protecting oxygen delivery can both matter.
Demonstrate an unambiguous control exchange, then explain how you would manage a student fixation on an EFB.
takeaways: Fitness changes faster than certification status.
Protect oxygen delivery when hypoxia and hyperventilation cannot be distinguished confidently.
Use reliable references and independent checks when sensations or expectations are misleading.
Legal alcohol limits do not define safe personal limits.

quiz.question: A pilot holds a valid medical certificate but slept three hours and feels unable to concentrate. Which decision best addresses the actual risk?
options: Fly because the certificate is current.
Replace the sleep with coffee and keep the itinerary.
Delay or cancel until adequate fitness is restored.
Fly only below the oxygen-requirement altitudes.
feedback: A certificate does not establish alertness on the day of flight.
Caffeine may reduce sleepiness temporarily without restoring adequate performance.
Changing the plan removes the immediate fatigue exposure before workload rises.
Altitude limits do not correct fatigue-related impairment.
quiz.hint: Separate eligibility paperwork from today’s ability to manage workload.

quiz.question: At altitude a pilot is breathing rapidly, feels tingling, and has trouble reasoning. Why is simply shutting off oxygen an unsafe response?
options: Rapid breathing proves that oxygen supply is excessive.
Hypoxia and hyperventilation can produce overlapping symptoms.
Oxygen prevents all carbon dioxide loss.
Hyperventilation is caused only by a failed oxygen regulator.
feedback: Rapid breathing can reduce carbon dioxide even when oxygen supply is inadequate.
The overlap requires protection of oxygen delivery while breathing and equipment are addressed.
Breathing rate and depth still affect carbon dioxide elimination.
Stress can cause excessive ventilation with normally operating equipment.
quiz.hint: Consider what the symptoms establish, and what they cannot establish.

quiz.question: A pilot plans a flight at 9,000 feet MSL after a scuba dive that required no decompression stop. Which FAA minimum waiting recommendation applies?
options: At least 24 hours after any scuba dive.
At least 12 hours because no stop was required.
No waiting if cabin altitude stays below 8,000 feet.
Eight hours if a medical certificate is current.
feedback: The planned actual flight altitude is above 8,000 feet, for which FAA guidance recommends at least 24 hours after any dive.
The 12-hour recommendation concerns qualifying dives followed by flight to actual altitudes up to 8,000 feet.
FAA diving guidance uses actual flight altitude because a pressurized aircraft can decompress.
The alcohol waiting rule and medical certification do not determine nitrogen elimination.
quiz.hint: Use actual flight altitude, not the cabin setting.

quiz.question: On a dark departure, acceleration creates a strong sensation that the nose is pitching up. What is the safest basis for checking whether that sensation is true?
options: The apparent pressure against the seatback.
The runway lights disappearing behind the airplane.
An immediate forward control input.
A disciplined cross-check of reliable flight instruments.
feedback: Seat pressure is influenced by acceleration and can reinforce the illusion.
The visual scene during departure may lack a dependable attitude reference.
Reacting to the sensation alone can create an actual unsafe descent.
The instrument cross-check supplies an independent reference for attitude and flight path.
quiz.hint: Seek a reference that does not depend on the same acceleration sensation.

quiz.question: You hear an aircraft report final and see a different aircraft farther out. What most directly reduces confirmation bias before turning base?
options: Assume the visible aircraft made the call.
Verify the reported position, distance, altitude, and other traffic.
Stop scanning and enlarge the traffic display.
Announce that the runway will be clear by your arrival.
feedback: One matching observation does not exclude another aircraft closer to the runway.
Independent checks test whether the initial interpretation is actually supported.
Display traffic can omit aircraft and does not replace an external scan.
A prediction does not establish the positions or intentions of other traffic.
quiz.hint: Look for evidence that could disprove your first interpretation.

quiz.question: A crewmember’s blood alcohol concentration is exactly 0.04 g/dL, nine hours after drinking, and the person reports feeling normal. What does 91.17 require?
options: The flight is allowed because eight hours elapsed.
The flight is allowed because 0.04 is included in the permitted range.
The person may not act or attempt to act as a crewmember.
The person may fly if another pilot agrees to monitor.
feedback: Elapsed time is only one of the rule’s independent restrictions.
The rule prohibits an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater.
Exactly 0.04 meets the prohibited concentration threshold regardless of the other stated facts.
Monitoring by another pilot does not remove a regulatory restriction.
quiz.hint: Check whether the threshold says greater than or greater than or equal to.
